source.title: Find the Count of Numbers Which Are Not Special

teaching.hint: How do divisors pair up, and when can a divisor be its own partner?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Exactly two proper divisors means exactly three total divisors; these numbers are precisely squares of primes.
solution_outline.approach: Sieve primes up to the exact integer square root of r. Count those whose squares lie in [l,r], then subtract this count from r-l+1.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: Each inspected prime contributes one special number exactly when its square lies in the requested inclusive range.
solution_outline.correctness: Divisors pair as d and x/d, so three total divisors require a self-paired square root m. A composite m supplies an additional divisor of m², so m must be prime. Conversely, a prime square has exactly divisors 1,p,p². Thus prime-square enumeration is both necessary and sufficient, and subtracting from the interval size counts precisely nonspecial values.
solution_outline.complexity: O(sqrt(r) log log sqrt(r)) time and O(sqrt(r)) auxiliary sieve space.
solution_outline.pitfall: Not every square is special: a composite root creates extra divisors; one itself has no proper divisors.

common_wrong_turns: Not every square is special: a composite root creates extra divisors; one itself has no proper divisors.
source_fidelity_notes: Retained proper-divisor exclusion of x, inclusive endpoints, positive range, and nonspecial rather than special output.
